what_its_for: Erythromycin is an antibiotic used to treat many types of bacterial infections, including chest infections, throat infections (strep throat), skin infections, ear infections, and sexually transmitted infections like chlamydia. It may also be used if you are allergic to penicillin. Remember: it only works on bacterial infections and will NOT treat colds, flu, or other viral illnesses.
how_to_take: Take erythromycin exactly as your doctor or pharmacist tells you. Swallow tablets or capsules whole — do not crush or chew them. Most forms work best when taken on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal), but if it upsets your stomach, you may take it with food. If you have a liquid (suspension), shake the bottle well before each use and measure carefully with the provided dosing spoon or syringe — never use a regular kitchen spoon. Finish the entire course of antibiotics your doctor prescribed, even if you feel better early. Stopping too soon can allow the infection to come back or become resistant to treatment.
dosing: The dose depends on your age, weight, and the type of infection being treated. A common adult dose is 250 mg to 500 mg taken every 6 hours (4 times a day), or 333 mg every 8 hours (3 times a day), for 7 to 14 days. For children, the dose is based on body weight and is determined by your doctor. Always follow the specific dose your doctor or pharmacist has given you and do not change it on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can increase your risk of side effects.
storage: Store erythromycin tablets and capsules at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C), away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep it out of the bathroom. Liquid erythromycin (suspension) may need to be refrigerated — check your label or ask your pharmacist. Keep all medications out of the reach of children and pets. Do not use the medication past the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium at the same time as erythromycin, as they can reduce how well the drug works — space them apart by at least 2 hours. Do not take erythromycin with certain other medications without checking with your doctor or pharmacist, especially: warfarin (blood thinner), statins like simvastatin or lovastatin, colchicine, digoxin, certain antihistamines (like terfenadine or astemizole), and some migraine or seizure medications, as dangerous interactions can occur. Avoid alcohol during your treatment course, as it may worsen side effects. Do not take any new prescription or over-the-counter medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements without asking your doctor or pharmacist first.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to an emergency room if you experience: severe stomach pain, cramping, or bloody/watery diarrhea (which could be a serious gut infection called C. difficile); fast, irregular, or pounding heartbeat or chest pain (rare but serious heart rhythm problems); yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe nausea/vomiting (signs of liver problems); hearing loss or ringing in your ears; severe skin rash, hives, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing (signs of a serious allergic reaction). Also call your doctor if your symptoms do not improve within a few days of starting the medication.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting erythromycin. However, it is very important to keep taking the full course as prescribed, even if you feel completely better, to make sure the infection is fully treated and to prevent it from coming back or becoming harder to treat.
special_populations: Older adults and people with liver problems should use erythromycin with caution, as the drug is processed by the liver — your doctor may adjust your dose. Erythromycin is generally considered safe to use during pregnancy when needed, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Erythromycin can pass into breast milk in small amounts, so let your doctor know if you are breastfeeding. For children, the dose will be carefully calculated based on your child's weight — follow your doctor's or pharmacist's instructions precisely.
